series.name: Greener Grass
series.tagline: The grass is always greener on the other side. Until you hear the water bill.
series.concept: Set in one neighborhood in an Indian city, Greener Grass follows ~15 interconnected characters — neighbors, colleagues, friends, family — each embodying a trait the world either envies or pities. Each episode peels back the surface to reveal the hidden cost of every envied life and the hidden gift in every pitied one. Over 30 episodes, the same events unfold from different perspectives, and the audience realizes: nobody has it figured out.

episodes.title: The Big House

slides.text: Everyone on Nehru Street calls him Lucky. Vikram Malhotra. Biggest house on the block. German car. Two floors. Terrace garden.
The neighbors see the Diwali lights first. The new TV delivered every year. The maid, the cook, the driver. They say, 'Vikram ka toh life set hai.'
When Pappu at the paan shop says he can't afford his daughter's school fees, someone always says, 'Go ask Lucky bhai. Uske paas toh paisa hi paisa hai.'
Vikram eats dinner alone. Every single night. The dining table seats eight. He sits in the same chair. The cook leaves the food covered and goes home by 7.
Nobody visits without wanting something. A loan. A job. A donation. Last Diwali, 40 people came. Not one brought mithai. They all brought requests.

At 9 PM, Vikram stands at his terrace. He looks down at Pappu's shop. Four men sitting on plastic chairs, laughing, sharing chai. Pappu is telling a joke. Vikram watches for ten minutes. Then he goes back inside.
The richest man on the street would trade it all for one evening where someone visits just to sit.

episodes.synopsis: Everyone calls him Lucky. He lives in the biggest house on the street. But the biggest house has the emptiest dining table.
episodes.caption: Everyone envies the big house. Nobody sees the empty chairs. Who's the richest person you know — and when was the last time you visited them with nothing to ask for?

episodes.title: The Paan Shop Philosopher

slides.text: Pappu Bhai has run the same paan shop for 22 years. Same corner. Same tin box. Same stained fingers. People walk past him to get to Lucky's house.
His wife takes the bus. His kids share textbooks. Last monsoon, the shop roof leaked for three weeks before he could afford the repair. The neighbors say, 'Bechaara Pappu.'
Sunita Aunty once told her husband, 'Thank God we're not like Pappu's family.' She said it loud enough for Pappu to hear. He just smiled and made her paan with extra meetha.

But here's the thing about Pappu's shop. It's not a paan shop. It's the neighborhood's living room. Kavita comes after a bad day at work. Arjun comes when his parents fight. Even Vikram has come — once, at midnight, after his divorce was finalized.
Pappu doesn't give advice. He just listens. And somehow, by the time you finish your paan, you've solved your own problem. He sleeps at 10. No alarm. No pills. No 3 AM thoughts.

One night, Pappu closes his shop late. He looks up at the big house on the corner. Every window is lit. He thinks, 'If I had that kind of money, I'd finally have some peace.' He doesn't know Vikram is thinking the exact same thing about him.
The poor man envies the rich man's house. The rich man envies the poor man's sleep.

episodes.synopsis: Pappu runs the cheapest paan shop on Nehru Street. Everyone feels sorry for him. But he's the one person everyone trusts with their secrets.
episodes.caption: Everyone feels sorry for Pappu. Nobody feels sorry for Lucky. But who sleeps better tonight? Tag someone who has nothing and everything at the same time.

episodes.title: The Life of the Party

slides.text: Neha Sharma's phone has 43 unread messages right now. Three party invites. Two 'just checking in' texts. One 'we haven't met in SO long' guilt trip. It's only Tuesday.

At every gathering, Neha is the center. She remembers everyone's anniversary. She organizes Holi. She plans the surprise parties. Meera once said, 'I wish I had Neha's social life.' Meera has no idea.
People say, 'Neha is never alone.' They say it like it's a compliment. Like being wanted by everyone is a gift. Like having zero free evenings is a blessing.

Last month, Neha's dog died. She cried for two hours. Then she wiped her face and went to Ritu's birthday because she'd promised. Nobody at the party asked why her eyes were red. They just said, 'Neha! Finally! The party starts now!'

She can't cancel. She tried once. Three people called within an hour. 'Kya hua? Sab theek hai? Tu theek hai na?' Having a bad day isn't allowed when you're the popular one. Your sadness becomes everyone else's emergency.

One evening, Neha skips a party. She sits on her balcony. Across the street, she sees Meera reading a book alone, drinking chai, not a single notification lighting up her phone. Neha thinks, 'That looks like heaven.'
Everyone wants to be invited everywhere. Until everywhere becomes a cage with no door marked 'exit.'

episodes.synopsis: Neha is invited to every wedding, every birthday, every chai session. She hasn't had a quiet evening in four years.
episodes.caption: Neha is never alone. That's not a compliment — it's a sentence. Do you know someone who can't say no? Send this to them. They need permission to cancel tonight.

episodes.title: The Quiet One

slides.text: Meera Joshi moved to Nehru Street five years ago. In five years, she has attended exactly three neighborhood events. People say, 'She thinks she's too good for us.'
At the one Diwali party she attended, she sat in the corner the whole time. Didn't mingle. Didn't dance. Sunita Aunty told everyone the next day, 'Very proud type. Doesn't talk to anyone.'
Neha once tried to include her. 'Come na, it'll be fun!' Meera said, 'I'm okay, thanks.' Neha took it personally. The whole street heard about it.

Here's what Meera actually does at parties. She watches. She noticed Vikram checking his phone 14 times at the Diwali party — all messages from his lawyer. She noticed Arjun's hands shaking when his mother bragged about his marks. She noticed Neha's red eyes.
The next morning, Meera left a small note under Neha's door. No name. Just: 'It's okay to not be okay. Even at parties.' Neha kept that note. She still doesn't know who wrote it.

That night Neha sat on her balcony staring at Meera's window, thinking 'that looks like heaven.' She didn't know Meera was looking back, thinking, 'I wish someone would invite me and actually mean it.'
The popular one wants to disappear. The quiet one wants to be found. And they live twenty feet apart.

episodes.synopsis: Meera barely speaks at gatherings. The neighborhood thinks she's proud. She's actually the only one paying attention.
episodes.caption: The quiet person at the party isn't ignoring you. They're the only one actually seeing you. Tag the quiet one in your group — they probably already know why.

episodes.title: Mirror, Mirror

slides.text: When Tara Kapoor walks into a room, people stop talking. Men stare. Women compare. Her mother says, 'You're so lucky, beta. Doors open for beautiful people.'
She got the bank job on the first interview. The auto driver never overcharges her. The chai wala gives her extra. People say, 'Tara ka toh kaam ho jaata hai sirf shakal se.'
Kavita once said at Pappu's shop, 'If I looked like Tara, I'd have half the problems I have.' Four men nodded. Pappu didn't. He just kept folding paan.

Last week, Tara presented a cost-saving plan at work. Saved the company twelve lakhs. Her boss said, 'Great work, Tara. Also, can you present at the client dinner? They'll like... you know... a fresh face.' She went home and threw the presentation in the trash.
In 30 years, nobody has asked Tara, 'What do you think?' They ask what she's wearing. Where she got her hair done. Whether she's seeing someone. She reads more books than Arjun. Nobody knows.

One evening, Tara goes to Pappu's shop. Not for paan. Just to talk. Pappu asks, 'Aaj kaisi ho, Tara?' Not 'aaj kaisi lag rahi ho.' How are you, not how do you look. Her eyes fill up. She says, 'You're the first person who's asked me that this month.'
The whole world sees Tara. But nobody has ever looked at her.

episodes.synopsis: Tara Kapoor walks into a room and everything stops. Everyone assumes her life is easy. Nobody has ever asked her an interesting question.
episodes.caption: Beauty opens doors. But it also locks you inside a version of yourself that other people built. Do you know someone everyone sees but nobody really knows? This one's for them.

episodes.title: 100 Out of 100

slides.text: Arjun Iyer scored 98.6% in his boards. His photo was in the newspaper. His mother laminated the clipping. It's still on the fridge. He's 30 now. The clipping is still the most recent thing he's proud of.

Every aunty on Nehru Street has said this to their kid at least once: 'Arjun ko dekho. Kuch seekho.' He's an IIT graduate. Software job in Bangalore. Came back to be closer to parents. The neighborhood treats him like a trophy.

His parents tell Sahil's parents, 'Arjun is working on something big.' They tell Pappu, 'He's considering an MBA abroad.' They tell Sunita Aunty, 'Companies are lining up.' Arjun hasn't changed his job title in four years.

Arjun wanted to start a food blog last year. He loves cooking. He wrote 15 posts. Published zero. Because what if it's not perfect? What if people say, 'The IIT guy writes about rajma chawal?' He deleted the drafts.

Sahil — the 'lazy' one — started a YouTube channel last month. It's terrible. Five subscribers. Sahil doesn't care. Arjun watches every video. He thinks, 'I wish I could do something without it having to be great.'

At Pappu's shop, Sahil's dad tells Arjun's dad, 'You're so lucky. My boy has no ambition.' Arjun's dad smiles proudly. He doesn't know that Arjun cried in the bathroom last Tuesday because he can't remember the last time he did something just for fun.
He was so afraid of scoring less than 100 that he stopped taking tests altogether.

episodes.synopsis: Arjun topped every exam. Now he's 30, stuck in a safe job, terrified of trying anything because the world only knows him as 'the brilliant one.'
episodes.caption: The smartest kid in the room grew up to be the most stuck. Perfection isn't a gift — it's a cage with a lock on the inside. Know someone who's brilliant but frozen? Send this.

episodes.title: Slow and Steady

slides.text: Bala has been at Kavita's company for six years. He is always the last one to finish anything. The office group chat has a running joke: 'Bala time' means twice the deadline.
In meetings, Bala speaks last. Sometimes not at all. Kavita's business partner once said, 'Why do we keep him? He's not slow — he's stalled.' Everyone laughed. Bala was in the next room. He heard.

His mother compares him to Arjun. 'That Iyer boy finished IIT in four years. You took six years to get a promotion.' Bala doesn't argue. He goes to his room and double-checks tomorrow's report. For the third time.

Three months ago, the company signed a vendor contract. Everyone approved it in one meeting. Bala asked for two more days. Nobody wanted to wait. He read it anyway. Page 34, clause 7B: a penalty clause that would've cost them 1.2 crores if they missed one delivery date.

Kavita called him into her office. She didn't say 'great catch.' She said, 'How did nobody else see this?' Bala said, 'They did see it. They just didn't read it.' He went back to his desk. Nobody made a Bala Time joke that week.
That evening, Arjun asked Bala at Pappu's shop, 'Doesn't it bother you? Being the slow one?' Bala sipped his chai and said, 'Does it bother you being the fast one?' Arjun didn't have an answer.
Everyone wants to be the fastest. Nobody wants to be the one who reads page 34.

episodes.synopsis: Bala takes three times longer than anyone else. His colleagues joke about him. But he sees things nobody else bothers to look at.
episodes.caption: The slow one saved the company. The fast ones almost sank it. Speed is overrated. Thoroughness is underrated. Tag the slow, careful one in your group — they're probably saving you right now.

episodes.title: The Art of Doing Nothing

slides.text: Sahil Khanna is 29. He's had seven jobs. Quit all of them. His father introduces him at gatherings as 'my younger one' — never by name, never with details.
The neighbors have a theory: 'Sahil has no drive.' Sunita Aunty has a stronger one: 'Uss ladke ka kuch nahi hoga.' When Arjun got his promotion, Sahil's mother locked herself in her room for an hour.

At Pappu's shop, the dads talk. 'My son cleared GATE.' 'My son is in Dubai.' When it's Sahil's dad's turn, he says, 'Sahil is... exploring options.' Pappu catches the tremor in his voice. Says nothing.

But here's what nobody talks about. Sahil goes for a walk every morning at 6. He reads for two hours after lunch. He started a YouTube channel about street food that makes him laugh. He sleeps at 10 and wakes up without an alarm.

He's not on any medication. He doesn't wake up at 3 AM wondering if he's enough. He doesn't compare his LinkedIn to anyone's. Last month, his therapist said, 'I wish more of my patients had your relationship with themselves.' Sahil said, 'I don't have a therapist.' She said, 'Exactly.'

Arjun watches Sahil's YouTube videos in secret. Five subscribers, terrible lighting, but Sahil is grinning in every one. Arjun thinks, 'He failed at everything and he's happier than me.' He almost comments. Then deletes it. The IIT guy can't be seen watching the dropout's channel.
The world calls him lazy. He calls it freedom. The difference is just who's keeping score.

episodes.synopsis: Sahil Khanna hasn't held a job for more than a year. His parents have given up. He's the only one sleeping eight hours a night without medication.
episodes.caption: Everyone's running a race. Sahil stopped to ask who set the finish line. Sometimes the most radical thing you can do is nothing. Tag the 'lazy' friend who's actually figured it out.

episodes.title: Morning Prayers

slides.text: Every morning at 5, while Nehru Street sleeps, one man walks to the Hanuman temple at the corner. Ramprasad Uncle. Seventy years old. Rain or shine. He hasn't missed a day in twelve years.

Sahil once said, 'Ramprasad Uncle lives in a different century.' Kavita said, 'He's a sweet old man, but come on — every day?' At Holi, the younger crowd avoids him because he always starts with 'Bhagwan ka ashirwad...'
His own son, who lives in Pune, calls once a month. 'Papa, you don't need to go to temple every day. Do yoga. Go for walks.' Ramprasad says, 'Beta, I am going for a walk. Just with better company.'

When the pandemic hit, Nehru Street panicked. Kavita's business nearly collapsed. Neha had three anxiety attacks in one week. Arjun stopped eating for two days. Ramprasad Uncle cooked khichdi for seven families. He didn't panic. He said, 'I've been preparing for the worst every morning for twelve years.'

His prayer isn't about God. It's about discipline. About standing still when everything shakes. About doing one thing every day that nobody asks you to do, so that when the world falls apart, you've already practiced being steady.

Kavita came to thank him after. She said, 'Uncle, I'm sorry I never took you seriously.' He said, 'Beta, I didn't do it for seriousness. I did it because the morning is quiet and the chai at the temple is free.' She laughed for the first time in weeks.
Everyone mocked the man who prepared for storms. Until it rained.

episodes.synopsis: Ramprasad Uncle goes to the temple at 5 AM every day. The neighborhood thinks he's out of touch. When crisis hit, he was the only one standing.
episodes.caption: They called him old-fashioned. He called it preparation. When the world shook, he was the only one who didn't fall. Tag someone whose quiet discipline saved everyone around them.

episodes.title: The Corner Office

slides.text: Kavita Reddy started her company with 80,000 rupees and a laptop. Seven years later, 50 people work for her. The neighborhood calls her 'Nehru Street ki businesswoman.' She calls herself 'tired.'

At parties, men shake her hand differently. Like she's won something. Women say, 'You're such an inspiration.' Sunita Aunty says, 'If only my daughter had that ambition.' Nobody asks what ambition costs.
Her Instagram has 12,000 followers. Photos of her at conferences. Team outings. Award ceremonies. What Instagram doesn't show: she missed her mother's birthday. Twice.

Her employees take Diwali week off. She works. They take sick leave. She works. Last month, two employees quit on the same day. She spent the night rewriting their code herself. Nobody at home to tell.

Bala is the only one who stays late with her sometimes. He doesn't say anything. Just works. One night, he left a cup of chai on her desk with a sticky note: 'Go home, ma'am. The code will still be broken tomorrow.' She laughed. Then she stayed.

On Sundays, Kavita drives past Sahil's house. He's on the balcony every time, reading, no rush. She thinks, 'What must that be like — a life with no one depending on you?' She doesn't know Sahil thinks the same about her: 'What must it be like — a life where you matter that much?'
She built a company where everyone can rest. Except her.

episodes.synopsis: Kavita runs the biggest company on Nehru Street. Her employees take two weeks off every year. She can't remember her last vacation.
episodes.caption: She gave 50 people their livelihood. Who gives her a day off? Being the boss isn't a privilege — it's a promise that never expires. Tag someone running a business who forgot to live.

episodes.title: Everything For the Kids

slides.text: Sunita Aunty was the best English teacher at DPS for eight years. Then her first child came. Then the second. She quit. The principal begged her to stay. She said, 'My children need me more.' That was fifteen years ago.

Now her son is in engineering college. Her daughter topped the state in her 10th boards. At every PTA meeting, the other parents say, 'Sunita ji, aapne toh kamaal kar diya.' She smiles the same smile every time.

The couple next door — the Jains — no children. Travel twice a year. Sunita once said to Pappu, 'Must be nice, having no responsibilities.' She said it breezy, like a joke. Pappu heard what was underneath.

Last month, her son came home for the weekend. He spent it in his room. On his phone. She made his favorite food — chole bhature — and waited at the dining table for forty minutes. He ate in his room. She ate alone.

She finds her old lesson plans sometimes, in a box under the bed. Neatly handwritten. Shakespeare. Premchand. Tenses and poetry. She reads them like love letters from another life. Then she closes the box and starts dinner.

What Sunita doesn't know: the Jains next door watch her kids come home every weekend and think, 'At least she has someone to cook for.' Mrs. Jain once made two cups of chai by accident. Force of habit from visiting her sister's house. She sat alone and drank both.
She gave them everything. They took it and grew up. That was the whole point. It just wasn't supposed to hurt this much.

episodes.synopsis: Sunita Aunty left her teaching career to raise her children. She's proud. She's also haunted by the life she didn't live.
episodes.caption: She raised them to fly. Nobody told her the nest would feel this empty. Every parent gives up a piece of themselves. Most of them never get it back. Send this to your mom. Call her after.

episodes.title: The Bench

slides.text: Every evening at 5:30, Sharma Ji sits on the concrete bench near the park. Same spot. Same white kurta. Same steel flask of chai. He's been doing this for twenty years. Since his wife passed.

The neighborhood feels sorry for him. 'Bechaare Sharma Ji. Alone all day. Kids in America. What a life.' Neha once brought him cake on his birthday. He said, 'Thank you, beta. But it's not my birthday.' It was. He just didn't want the pity.

Ramprasad once said, 'Sharma Ji should come to the temple. He needs community.' Kavita once said, 'He should volunteer somewhere. Stay busy.' Everyone has a plan for the old man. Nobody has asked the old man if he has his own.

From this bench, Sharma Ji sees everything. He saw Vikram sit in his car for twenty minutes before going inside — afraid of the empty house. He saw Neha cancel a plan and then panic-call three people. He saw Arjun throw away a sketchbook in the dustbin last Thursday.

He's not lonely. He's the only one on this street who has nothing left to prove, nothing left to want, and nobody left to impress. When you remove all of that, what's left is just... watching. And it turns out, watching is the most peaceful thing a person can do.

Last week, Deepak — the quiet one nobody notices — sat next to Sharma Ji without saying anything. They shared chai for twenty minutes. Then Deepak said, 'You see everything, don't you?' Sharma Ji said, 'Only because nobody sees me.'
Everyone rushes past the bench. The bench sees everyone.

episodes.synopsis: Sharma Ji sits on the same bench every evening. Everyone thinks he's lonely. He's been watching the whole neighborhood like a silent film.
episodes.caption: Everyone feels sorry for the old man on the bench. He feels sorry for all of them. Stillness isn't loneliness — it's a front-row seat to the whole show. Sit with someone silent today.

episodes.title: Monday Morning

slides.text: Rohan Das had a corner office at a consulting firm. AC. Good salary. Provident fund. One Monday morning, he walked in, placed his resignation letter on his boss's desk, and said, 'I'm going to paint.' His boss said, 'Walls?' Rohan said, 'Canvas.'

The neighborhood verdict was unanimous: pagal hai. His father didn't speak to him for four months. His mother cried. Sunita Aunty told everyone, 'He had everything and threw it away.' Kavita said, 'He'll come back in six months.'

It's been two years. He rents a small room near the market. Sells paintings at exhibitions. Some months are good. Most months are not. His LinkedIn still says 'Consultant' because his mother asked him not to change it.
Every Monday morning at 7 AM, Rohan wakes up, makes chai, puts on music, and paints. No alarm. No dread. No Sunday-night anxiety. He is the only person on Nehru Street who doesn't hate Mondays.

Last month, Kavita bought one of his paintings for her office. She didn't tell anyone. It hangs behind her desk — a green landscape, a bench, a man watching a sunset. She looks at it when the day gets too heavy. She hasn't connected the irony yet.

Rohan visits Pappu's shop on Saturday evenings. One night, Arjun was there. Arjun said, 'Weren't you scared? Leaving everything?' Rohan said, 'I was terrified. But I was more scared of being 60 and still wondering what if.' Arjun went home and opened a blank document. He didn't write anything. But he didn't close it either.
They called him crazy for leaving. Nobody asks why the rest of them stay.

episodes.synopsis: Rohan left a 15 LPA job to become a painter. His family disowned his choice. His Monday mornings are the only ones worth envying.
episodes.caption: He left the safe path. They stayed. Everyone called him crazy. Nobody asked themselves why staying felt like drowning. Tag someone who needs permission to follow the crazy dream.

episodes.title: The Invisible Man

slides.text: Ask anyone on Nehru Street about Deepak and they'll say, 'Deepak? Which one? Oh, the... uh... he lives near the water tank, right?' That's it. That's his entire reputation.

He works at a government office. Not high rank, not low rank. Middle. He got married at 28 to a girl his parents chose. It wasn't love. It wasn't arranged drama. It was just... fine. Everything about Deepak is just fine.

At parties, he's the one standing near the food table, not talking to anyone special, not being missed by anyone. Neha doesn't have his number. Kavita doesn't know what he does. Arjun has forgotten his last name. Twice.

But here's what being invisible gives you: peace. Nobody expects anything from Deepak. Nobody compares their kids to him. Nobody writes about him in WhatsApp groups. When he fails, nobody notices. When he succeeds, nobody cares. And that — strangely — is freedom.

He takes his kid to the park every Sunday. Not because he's a 'devoted father.' Just because he likes it. He doesn't post about it. Nobody gives him an award for it. He just does it and goes home and that's enough.

Remember — Deepak is the one who sat next to Sharma Ji on the bench. No agenda. No need. Just sat. Sharma Ji said, 'You see everything, don't you?' Deepak said, 'No. I just don't need to be seen.' Sharma Ji poured him more chai.
In a world where everyone is trying to be someone, he found peace in being no one.

episodes.synopsis: Deepak has no standout talent, no dramatic story. In a neighborhood of extremes, he's the only one nobody envies, nobody pities, and nobody watches. And he's fine.
episodes.caption: Nobody writes stories about the average guy. Maybe that's the whole point. Not every life needs a plot twist. Some lives are just... good. Tag your Deepak. They probably won't care. That's why they're Deepak.

episodes.title: The Diwali Party

slides.text: Once a year, Nehru Street has a Diwali party in the park. Everyone comes. The rich and the poor. The busy and the idle. The loud and the quiet. For one night, they're all in one place. But they're not at the same party.

Vikram arrives and everyone greets him. 'Lucky bhai! Diwali mubarak!' But watch closely — every greeting has a follow-up. 'Bhai, wanted to talk about that loan.' 'Vikram sir, my son needs a reference.' By the third handshake, his smile is a mask.

Neha is organizing the music, the food, the seating. She's been here since 4 PM. Everyone says, 'What would we do without Neha?' She hasn't eaten. She hasn't sat down. She watches Meera arrive alone, sit on the wall, open a book. Neha thinks, 'One hour. Just one hour of that.'

From Meera's wall, the whole party is a painting. She sees Arjun flinch when his mother says 'mera beta, IIT' to a stranger. She sees Sahil eat three plates of food without guilt. She sees Kavita check her phone eleven times. She sees Tara dodge two men who want selfies. She sees Ramprasad quietly light a diya for his wife.

At 9 PM, the fireworks start. For thirty seconds, nobody's performing. Nobody's envying. Nobody's hiding. Everyone looks up. Vikram stands next to Pappu. Neha stops moving. Meera puts her book down. Sharma Ji smiles. For thirty seconds, they're all just people watching the sky.

Then the fireworks end. The masks go back on. Vikram reaches for his phone. Neha asks who needs chai. Arjun stands behind his mother. Meera opens her book. Thirty seconds of truth. That's all any of them can handle.
Fifteen people at one party. Fifteen different evenings. The only moment they shared was the one where nobody was trying to be anything.

episodes.synopsis: The annual Nehru Street Diwali celebration. Every character is here. We see the same evening through Vikram's eyes, Neha's eyes, and Meera's eyes. Same party. Three different realities.
episodes.caption: You've been to this party. You've been one of these people. Everyone was there. Nobody was at the same party. Which character did you watch? Tell me in the comments.

episodes.title: The Unmarried One

slides.text: Priya Menon is 35. She is not married. That one sentence has generated more neighborhood discussion than Vikram's divorce, Kavita's company, and Rohan's career change combined.
Sunita Aunty has a theory: 'Too choosy.' Arjun's mother has another: 'Career ke chakkar mein late ho gayi.' Vikram's mother said the worst one: 'Koi kami hogi.' Something must be wrong with her.
At the Diwali party, three different aunties asked her the same question within one hour: 'So, koi hai life mein?' Priya smiled and said, 'Haan, main hoon.' Nobody laughed. They didn't understand.

Priya runs a content agency from home. She has savings. A flat she bought herself. A cat named Kafka. She cooks when she wants, orders in when she doesn't. She went to Portugal alone last year and didn't post a single photo.

Sunita Aunty cries on the phone to her sister about her husband's indifference. Vikram eats alone. Neha can't sit still for five minutes. And yet they all look at Priya and think, 'poor thing.' She looks at them and thinks nothing. She's too busy reading.

Tara came over once. They sat on the balcony drinking chai. Tara said, 'Doesn't it get lonely?' Priya said, 'Sometimes. Does it get lonely being surrounded by people who only see your face?' Tara stayed till midnight. First real conversation she'd had in months.
They keep asking when she's going to settle down. She settled down years ago. They just don't recognize it without a wedding card.

episodes.synopsis: Priya is 35 and unmarried. The questions never stop. But she's the most settled person on Nehru Street.
episodes.caption: She doesn't fit the template. That's not a failure — it's a choice. 'Settled' doesn't mean married. It means knowing who you are and being okay with it. Tag the single friend who has it figured out.

episodes.title: Lucky's Son

slides.text: The results came out on a Tuesday. By Wednesday morning, the whole street knew. Vikram Malhotra's son — the boy with tutors, coaching classes, and every advantage money can buy — failed. Two subjects. Red marks on the marksheet.

Sunita Aunty said, 'Money can't buy everything.' Arjun's mother said, 'See? Our Arjun did it on his own merit.' Three people sent 'condolence' messages to Vikram that were really disguised gloating. The street was sympathetic the way wolves are sympathetic to a limping deer.
Pappu heard the chatter at his shop all day. 'Lucky ka luck finally ran out.' 'Itna paisa, phir bhi fail.' Pappu made everyone their paan and said nothing. He remembered something nobody else did.

Vikram's son didn't fail because he's stupid. He failed because his parents were getting divorced during his exams, the house was a battlefield, and he spent most nights sleeping with headphones on to drown out the arguments. Nobody at school knew. Nobody on the street knew.

Pappu knew. Because two months ago, the boy came to the paan shop at 11 PM. Didn't want paan. Just sat on the plastic chair and said, 'Pappu bhai, ghar mein bahut shor hai.' Pappu gave him chai and let him sit till midnight. He didn't tell a soul.

Arjun's mother bragged about Arjun's marks that whole week. Arjun found the boy's Instagram — a private account, 40 followers, full of sketches and poems. Really good ones. Arjun thought, 'He failed at the thing that doesn't matter. He's brilliant at the thing that does.'
A boy failed an exam. The whole street had an opinion. Not one person asked him how he was doing.

episodes.synopsis: Vikram's son fails his 12th board exams. The neighborhood reacts with shock — not sympathy, but the quiet satisfaction of seeing the mighty stumble.
episodes.caption: He failed the exam. The neighborhood celebrated quietly. Nobody knew about the war at home. Before you judge someone's result, ask about their process. Tag someone who judges without asking.

episodes.title: The Resignation

slides.text: On a Thursday morning, Kavita Reddy called an all-hands meeting. She stood in front of 50 people and said, 'I'm taking a three-month leave. Bala will handle operations.' The room went silent. Not the respectful kind. The scared kind.
The street found out by evening. Vikram said, 'She's selling.' Neha said, 'She's burned out.' Sunita Aunty said, 'This is what happens when women try to do too much.' Nobody guessed the real reason.

'Why Bala?' the employees asked. The guy who takes forever? The slowest worker in the company? Kavita's business partner called it 'professional suicide.' Three employees updated their LinkedIn that night.

Three days before the announcement, Kavita fainted in her bathroom. She told nobody. She drove herself to the hospital. The doctor said, 'Your body is shutting down from stress. How long have you been sleeping three hours a night?' She said, 'About two years.'

She chose Bala because Bala is the only person who never rushed. Who read every page. Who stayed late not to impress her, but because the work wasn't done. She told him privately, 'Everyone thinks you're slow. I think you're the only one who's careful.' Bala said, 'I'll read every page, ma'am. As always.'

That night, Kavita went to Pappu's shop. She didn't order anything. She sat on the plastic chair and said, 'I'm tired, Pappu bhai. Really tired.' Pappu said, 'Then rest, beta. The shop doesn't close because I take a break. Neither will yours.'
The strongest person on the street finally did the bravest thing she could: she sat down.

episodes.synopsis: Kavita announces she's stepping back from her own company. Everyone is stunned. Bala is the only one who's not surprised.
episodes.caption: Walking away from what you built isn't weakness. It's the hardest kind of strength. Kavita didn't quit. She rested. There's a difference. Tag someone who needs permission to stop.

episodes.title: The Homecoming

slides.text: The call came on a Sunday. 'Papa, we're moving back. Closer to you. We found a flat ten minutes away.' Ramprasad said, 'Bahut accha, beta.' He hung up and sat in his puja room for an hour. He wasn't praying. He was processing.
The news spread fast. 'Ramprasad ji's son is coming back!' Sunita Aunty said, 'Finally, he won't be alone.' Pappu said, 'Good for him.' Sharma Ji said nothing. He knew.

Everyone imagined a Bollywood reunion. The son touching the father's feet. Grandchildren running in the garden. Ramprasad Uncle finally not eating alone. The neighborhood wanted a happy ending for the old man.

Ramprasad hasn't lived with anyone in nine years. He eats at 7. His son's family eats at 9. He sleeps at 9:30. The grandchildren sleep at 11. His routine — the one thing that kept him sane — is about to be dismantled.

He told Sharma Ji on the bench. 'I prayed for this for years. Now it's happening and I'm scared.' Sharma Ji said, 'When my wife was alive, I wanted quiet. Now I'd give everything for one loud evening.' Ramprasad went home and cleared the spare room.

The night before his son arrived, Ramprasad went to the temple at midnight. Not his usual time. Pappu's shop was still open. Pappu called out, 'Subah nahi aaoge kya, Uncle?' Ramprasad said, 'Kal se subah mein cartoons hain.'
He prayed for years for his family to come home. He forgot to pray for the courage to let his peace be disrupted by love.

episodes.synopsis: Ramprasad Uncle's son announces he's moving back from Pune. The neighborhood thinks it's wonderful. Ramprasad isn't sure his quiet life can survive it.
episodes.caption: He wanted them home. Now they're coming and he's terrified. Because peace is easy when you're alone. The real test is keeping it when the house is full. Relate? Share this.

episodes.title: Where Is Tara?

slides.text: For fourteen days, Tara Kapoor didn't leave her house. Her lights were on. Her car was parked. But the girl everyone stared at had become invisible. And the strangest part? Almost nobody noticed.
After a week, someone noticed. Sunita Aunty said, 'Tara hasn't come to the market.' Neha sent a text: 'Hey, long time! All good?' Three heart emojis. No real question. No follow-up.
The theories: 'Breakup.' 'She's getting work done — you know, cosmetic.' 'I heard she's seeing someone secretly.' Every theory was about her body or her love life. Not one was about her mind.

Tara was depressed. Not the Instagram kind. The real kind. The kind where you shower sitting down. Where daylight feels like noise. Where the mirror — the thing everyone told her was her greatest asset — became the thing she couldn't look at.

Pappu knew. Because she'd told him three months ago, late at night. 'I feel like I'm disappearing, Pappu bhai. Like the real me was never here.' He didn't tell anyone. He left a tiffin outside her door every evening for two weeks. Dal chawal. Nothing fancy. No note.

Meera noticed on day three. She saw the tiffin. She saw Pappu. She didn't say anything to anyone. She slipped a note under Tara's door: 'You don't have to open the door. Just know someone's on the other side.' Same handwriting as the note she'd left Neha.
The whole street stared at Tara for years. When she needed to be seen, only two people were looking.

episodes.synopsis: Tara disappears from public life for two weeks. The neighborhood has theories. Meera follows a hunch. Pappu keeps a secret.
episodes.caption: Depression doesn't look like sadness. It looks like absence. The most beautiful girl on the street disappeared and almost nobody noticed. Pay attention to the people who stop showing up. They need you most.

episodes.title: Publish

slides.text: It took Arjun Iyer fourteen months, thirty-seven deleted drafts, and one conversation with Rohan to finally press publish. A food blog. About rajma chawal. At 2 AM on a Wednesday, when no one was watching.

By morning, twelve people had read it. His mother didn't understand. 'You write about dal and rice? With your IIT degree?' His father forwarded it to three relatives with the caption: 'Arjun's hobby.' Hobby. The word stung.

At Pappu's shop, the talk was predictable. 'IIT se nikla aur food blog likh raha hai.' 'Waste of talent.' 'His parents must be so disappointed.' Pappu said, 'Maine padha. Rajma waali post acchi thi.' Nobody heard him.

Arjun checked his analytics every hour. Twelve readers. Then fifteen. Then fourteen — someone had left. He spiraled. 'I knew it. I should have kept it safe. I should have deleted it.' He almost did. Then a comment appeared.

The comment was from Sahil Khanna. The lazy one. The dropout. Five words: 'Bro, this made me hungry.' No analysis. No critique. Just a human being responding like a human being. Arjun stared at it for five minutes. Then he laughed. He actually laughed.

That evening, Arjun did something he'd never done before. He went to Sahil's YouTube channel and commented on a video. 'The dosa guy at 3:45 looks like our maths teacher.' Sahil replied in one minute: 'BRO. I literally thought the same thing.' Subscriber count: 6.
The IIT graduate was saved by the dropout's comment. The smartest kid on the street needed the simplest response. Sometimes 'this made me hungry' is enough.

episodes.synopsis: Arjun finally publishes his food blog. He expects mockery. The first real response comes from Sahil — the one he was too proud to engage with.
episodes.caption: He waited fourteen months to press publish. The thing that saved him wasn't a literary review. It was five words from the last person he expected. Be that person for someone today. Comment something real.

episodes.title: The Cancellation

slides.text: On a Monday, Neha Sharma sent the same message to fifteen people: 'Not feeling well. Can't make it. Sorry!' Fifteen different chats. Same lie. She wasn't sick. She was done.

The first day, people said, 'Neha's sick, get well soon!' The second day, 'Still sick? Should we visit?' The third day, 'She's probably just busy.' By day five, they'd moved on. The party found a new organizer.

Sunita Aunty said, 'She'll bounce back, she always does.' Vikram barely noticed — he had his own problems. Sahil said, 'Maybe she's finally resting.' Sahil was right, but nobody listened to him about anything.

Neha sat on her couch for three days in the same clothes. She watched the ceiling. Her dog lay beside her. She realized something awful: without planning events for other people, she had no idea what to do with herself.

On day six, there was a knock. Not a text. Not a call. A knock. Meera stood at the door with a container of tomato soup. She said, 'I'm not checking in. I'm not asking how you are. I'm just leaving this.' She placed it on the floor and walked away.

Neha drank the soup. Then she cried. Not because of the soup. Because in six days, out of the 200 people in her phone, one person showed up. And it was the 'arrogant' quiet girl she'd tried to fix for years.
200 contacts. 43 group chats. One knock on the door.

episodes.synopsis: Neha cancels everything for a week. The popular girl goes silent. Only Meera shows up — not with words, but with soup.
episodes.caption: 200 people in her phone. One showed up with soup. Being popular isn't the same as being loved. And the person you least expect might be the one who cares the most. Tag the person who'd bring you soup.

episodes.title: Five Subscribers

slides.text: Sahil's YouTube channel is called 'Sahil Khata Hai.' He films street food vendors. Shaky camera. Bad audio. Terrible thumbnails. He posts every Tuesday. He has never missed a Tuesday in eight months.

The street knows about the channel. They laugh about it. 'Sahil thinks he's a YouTuber.' Arjun's mother said, 'Even his YouTube is underperforming.' 500 subscribers in eight months. By Nehru Street's standards, that's failure.
His father stopped asking about the channel months ago. He asks about jobs instead. 'There's an opening at the bank. Just apply.' Sahil says, 'Tuesday ko shoot hai, Papa.' His father leaves the room.

But last month, something happened. Sahil filmed a chaat vendor who'd been working the same corner for 40 years. The video wasn't about food. It was about the man. His story. How he raised three kids from a pushcart. That video got 50,000 views. Sahil didn't make a rupee from it. The vendor's son started a GoFundMe.
Sahil's father saw the video. He didn't say anything to Sahil. But that night, he went to his room, found the newspaper with the bank job listing, and quietly threw it away.

At Pappu's shop, Sahil's dad sat quietly for the first time ever. When the other dads started bragging, he didn't shrink. Pappu noticed and said, 'Sahil ka video dekha?' The father nodded and said, 'Mera beta.' Not 'my younger one.' Not vaguely. Just — 'Mera beta.'
500 subscribers didn't make him successful. But it made his father say his name.

episodes.synopsis: Sahil's YouTube channel hits 500 subscribers. It's nothing by internet standards. It's everything by his.
episodes.caption: Success isn't a number. It's the moment someone who doubted you starts to see you. 500 subscribers and a father who finally said 'that's my son.' Sometimes that's the whole award. Tag your biggest supporter — even if they took a while to come around.

episodes.title: What Deepak Saw

slides.text: Deepak doesn't sleep well. Not from anxiety — just habit. He gets up at 2 AM most nights, drinks water, looks out the window. Most nights, there's nothing. Last Tuesday, there was something.
At 2:15 AM, Vikram's front gate opened. He walked out — no car, no driver, just him in kurta and chappals. He walked to the end of the street and sat on Sharma Ji's bench. Alone. In the dark.

Ten minutes later, another figure appeared. From the other direction. Kavita. Still in her office clothes at 2 AM. She saw Vikram on the bench and almost turned around. But she didn't. She sat on the other end. They didn't speak for twenty minutes.

Then Vikram said, 'Can't sleep either?' Kavita said, 'Haven't slept properly in two years.' He said, 'Same. The house is too quiet.' She said, 'The office is too loud.' He laughed. She laughed. Two people who run the street, sitting on a bench like lost kids.

They talked for an hour. About nothing important. About the chai at Pappu's shop. About Sharma Ji's bench being surprisingly comfortable. About how the street looks different at 2 AM — quieter, kinder, more honest. When they left, they didn't exchange numbers. They didn't need to. They both knew they'd be back.

Deepak watched the whole thing. He didn't tell his wife. He didn't tell Pappu. He didn't post it or gossip about it. He just thought, 'Everyone on this street is performing all day. The only honest hours are the ones nobody sees.' Then he went back to bed.
The invisible man saw the realest moment on Nehru Street. And kept it safe. Some things aren't meant to be shared. Just witnessed.

episodes.synopsis: Late one night, Deepak sees something from his window that connects two characters in a way nobody would expect. But he keeps it to himself.
episodes.caption: The most real moments happen when nobody's performing. At 2 AM, the masks come off. And the invisible man saw it all and kept it safe. What have you witnessed that you've never told anyone?

episodes.title: The New Neighbor

slides.text: The moving truck came on a Saturday. A young couple — Ankit and Riya, late 20s, freshly married, first flat. They stood at the gate with two suitcases and a mattress. They looked at Nehru Street and thought: 'We're going to love it here.'

Within a week, they had opinions. 'The guy in the big house? Set for life.' 'That girl Neha? So popular, yaar, I wish we had that energy.' 'The quiet woman upstairs seems stuck up.' 'The paan shop uncle is sweet but... sad situation.' Same street. Same wrong conclusions.

Riya said, 'If I had Tara's looks, I'd never worry about anything.' Ankit said, 'If I had Arjun's brain, I'd have cracked IAS by now.' They looked at every neighbor and saw what they wanted. Which is to say — they saw nothing at all.

They don't know Vikram eats alone. They don't know Neha cancelled everything for a week and one person showed up. They don't know Tara covered her mirrors. They don't know Sahil is happier than all of them. They don't know about the bench at 2 AM.

But you do. You've been watching for 24 episodes. You've seen behind every door. And here's the uncomfortable part: before you started watching, you were Ankit and Riya. You looked at your own neighbors the same way.

Ankit and Riya went to Pappu's shop on their first evening. Pappu made them paan with extra meetha and said, 'Nehru Street mein welcome. Yahan sab log acche hain.' Riya whispered to Ankit: 'What a simple man.' Pappu heard. He smiled. He's heard worse from people with more.
New eyes see old lies. The story isn't what the street looks like. It's what you learn when you stop looking and start sitting.

episodes.synopsis: A young couple moves into the empty flat on Nehru Street. They look at the neighborhood and see everything the audience saw in Episode 1 — before they knew the truth.
episodes.caption: Every new person on the street sees the same surface. You saw it too — in Episode 1. But now you know better. Or do you? Are you still making the same assumptions about people in YOUR life?

episodes.title: The Painting on the Wall

slides.text: Rohan asked the RWA for permission to paint the blank wall near the park. They said no. He painted it anyway. A mural — fifteen figures, all looking in different directions, each one standing in green grass. None of them looking at their own feet.

The street had opinions. Sunita Aunty: 'Who gave him permission?' Vikram: 'It's actually quite good.' Kavita: 'He should sell prints.' Arjun stared at it for ten minutes and recognized one of the figures — it was holding a blank notebook.

Neha saw a figure surrounded by people, looking exhausted. Tara saw one that everyone was staring at. Sahil saw one lying in the grass. Sharma Ji saw one sitting on a bench. Every character found themselves. None of them said it out loud.

Rohan painted them all. He knew. The artist who left everything had spent two years watching the street, and he'd seen what Meera sees, what Sharma Ji sees, what Deepak saw at 2 AM. He put it on a wall where everyone could see it and nobody could say it.

Meera brought him chai while he painted. She looked at the finished mural and said, 'You put yourself in here too.' Rohan pointed to a small figure in the corner, facing the wall instead of looking over the fence. He said, 'That's the only one who's happy.'

Ankit — the new neighbor — walked past the mural and said to Riya, 'Nice art. Doesn't mean anything though.' Pappu, overhearing from his shop, said under his breath, 'Give it time, beta. You'll find yourself on that wall too.'
Fifteen people on a wall. All looking at someone else's grass. The only honest one is facing his own.

episodes.synopsis: Rohan paints a mural on the neighborhood wall. Everyone sees something different in it. Because everyone sees their own story.
episodes.caption: Rohan put the whole street on a wall. Everyone saw themselves. Nobody admitted it. What would your figure be doing? Looking at someone else, or finally looking down at your own grass?

episodes.title: Surface Tension

slides.text: It started with a borrowed book. Tara knocked on Priya's door to return a Murakami novel. Priya said, 'Come in for chai?' Tara almost said no. Force of habit. Then she said, 'Actually, yes.'

If the neighbors could see inside, they'd say, 'The pretty one and the alone one, having sad-girl chai.' The neighbors can't imagine two women sitting together without it being about loneliness or gossip.

Tara said, 'People think my life is easy because of how I look.' Priya said, 'People think my life is incomplete because I'm alone.' Tara said, 'You're not alone, you have a cat named Kafka.' Priya said, 'Exactly. Clearly I'm fine.'

'They see your face,' Priya said. 'They see my finger,' she held up her ring finger, 'empty.' Tara said, 'What if we're the same person? Defined by one thing we didn't choose, judged by people who chose nothing.' They sat with that.

They talked until midnight. About books. About why Indian mothers weaponize food. About the Diwali party and how exhausting it was. About Meera's notes — Tara showed hers. Priya's eyes widened. 'She left me one too. After my mother's surgery. Same handwriting.'

As Tara left, she said, 'We should do this again.' Priya said, 'My door's open. Unlike my marital status.' Tara laughed so hard she snorted. They stood in the doorway like old friends. Two women the world defined by surfaces, finally finding depth.
The world put them in two boxes. 'Beautiful' and 'Single.' Turns out those boxes were right next to each other. They just needed to knock on the wall.

episodes.synopsis: Priya and Tara — the single one and the beautiful one — spend an evening together and discover they're fighting the same battle: being reduced to one thing.
episodes.caption: Two women the world reduced to one adjective each. They found each other over chai and a borrowed book. Connection doesn't come from group chats. It comes from someone saying 'actually, yes.' Tag your unexpected friendship.

episodes.title: The Notes

slides.text: You know about the notes. Neha got one after the Diwali party. Tara got one during her two weeks. Priya got one after her surgery. Unsigned. Same handwriting. Same simple truth. Everyone assumed it was an angel. It wasn't. It was Meera. And her reasons aren't pretty.

If people knew, they'd say, 'How sweet.' 'What a kind soul.' They'd turn her into the Quiet Hero. Another box. Another label. Meera doesn't write the notes because she's kind. She writes them because she can't do the other thing.

She saw Neha's red eyes at the party and wanted to walk over and say, 'I see you.' She couldn't. Her throat closed. Her legs didn't move. She went home and wrote the note instead. The note was her voice because her voice wouldn't come.

Meera isn't an introvert by choice. She's terrified. Of saying the wrong thing. Of being too much. Of being not enough. The quiet isn't peace — it's a wall she built at age 12 when her best friend told the whole class what she'd said in confidence. She hasn't trusted her own voice since.

So she watches. And writes. Anonymous care from a safe distance. The notes are love letters she'll never sign. Because signing them would mean being seen. And being seen is the one thing that terrifies the girl who sees everyone.

Until the soup. When she brought soup to Neha's door, she didn't write a note. She knocked. Her hand trembled. She left the soup and walked away fast, heart pounding. But she knocked. For the first time, she used her hand instead of her handwriting.
She's not the quiet hero. She's the scared girl who found a way to love people from behind a door. And one day, she knocked.

episodes.synopsis: Meera's been leaving anonymous notes for months. We finally learn why. It's not kindness. It's something more complicated and more human.
episodes.caption: The notes weren't kindness. They were fear dressed up as grace. The quiet one isn't at peace — she's fighting a war every day to connect. But she knocked. That's the whole story. Tag the quiet one who's braver than they know.

episodes.title: The Offer

slides.text: It came out of nowhere. Vikram walked into Pappu's shop on a Tuesday evening and said, 'I have a property in South City. Empty shop. Good area. I'll set you up. No rent for two years. You deserve better than this corner.'

The street found out in a day. 'Lucky bhai is relocating Pappu!' 'Pappu's life is about to change!' Sunita Aunty said, 'Dekho, this is what rich people should do.' Even Neha shared it in the group chat with clapping emojis.

Pappu's wife was excited. 'South City! The kids can go to a better school! We'll have AC!' She started packing before Pappu had even answered. She didn't understand why he was sitting on the charpoy, staring at the wall.

Pappu went to the shop at midnight. Sat on the plastic chair. Looked at the corner where Vikram's son once cried. The counter where Tara found her voice. The wall where Arjun leaned when he couldn't breathe. This wasn't a paan shop. This was the only place on Nehru Street where people were real.

He told Vikram the next day. 'Bhai, I can't.' Vikram didn't understand. 'But it's a better location. More money. More space.' Pappu said, 'Vikram bhai, you have a big house and nobody visits you without a reason. I have a small shop and everyone visits me without one. Which one of us should move?'

Vikram went home that night and sat at his dining table. Eight chairs. He picked up the phone and called Pappu. 'Tomorrow evening, can I come sit? Not for chai. Not for paan. Just to sit.' Pappu said, 'The chair is always here, bhai. Always was.'
The rich man offered to change the poor man's life. The poor man changed the rich man's instead.

episodes.synopsis: Vikram offers to set Pappu up in a bigger shop in a better area. Pappu says no. And for the first time, Vikram understands what richness actually means.
episodes.caption: He said no to a better shop because he already had the best location — in everyone's heart. Real wealth isn't what you own. It's who shows up without a reason. This one's for the Pappu in your life.

episodes.title: The Bench — Finale

slides.text: It's a Sunday evening. Golden hour. Sharma Ji is on his bench. Deepak sits beside him. The street is alive — Vikram at Pappu's shop, Neha walking slowly (for once), Meera on her balcony, Arjun typing on his laptop at the park. The whole cast, in one frame, just living.
Deepak said, 'Uncle, you've been watching this street for twenty years. What have you seen?' Sharma Ji poured two cups of chai from his flask and said, 'I'll tell you a story. About a garden.'

'Once there was a street where everyone had a garden. But nobody looked at their own. The rich man looked at the poor man's laughter. The poor man looked at the rich man's walls. The popular girl looked at the quiet girl's silence. The quiet girl looked at the popular girl's crowd.'

'The smart one looked at the lazy one's freedom. The lazy one looked at the smart one's respect. The boss looked at the artist's joy. The artist looked at the boss's security. The parent looked at the childless one's peace. The childless one looked at the parent's purpose.'

'One day, an old man sat on a bench and watched them all. He'd had a garden once. A wife. A family. A home full of noise. It was all gone now. And from his bench, he could see what none of them could: every garden was green. Every single one. They just never looked down.'

Deepak was quiet for a long time. Then he said, 'That's us. That's this whole street.' Sharma Ji nodded. 'Twenty years on this bench, beta. And the only thing I've learned is this: the grass was never greener anywhere. You were always standing on good ground. You were just looking at someone else's garden.'
Look down. Your grass is green enough.

episodes.synopsis: Sharma Ji. The bench. One evening. He tells Deepak the one story that ties the whole street together. The grass was never greener. You were just looking at someone else's garden.
episodes.caption: Thirty episodes. Fifteen lives. One street. One bench. One truth. The grass was never greener. You were just looking at someone else's garden. Thank you for sitting with Nehru Street. Now look down at your own grass.
